title: Unformed justifying faith means active faith birthing charity, not idle speculation (Vasquez)
source_text: XX. Caeterum quum dicunt Scholae Romanae Theologi fidem, etiam nondum formatam, justificantem esse suo modo, quoniam scilicet disponit ad justificationem, & est justitiae hominis coram Deo radix & fundamentum, per fidem nondum formatam non intelligunt fidem inertem atque otiosam, & quae mere speculativa sit; sed fidem quandam actuosam, & quae incipit esse per bona opera efficax, quaeque charitatem quodammodo parturit, & ad eam contendit, licet illam nondum adepta dici possit. Istud aperte docet Vasquez. Postremo, inquit, observandum est, quum dicimus fidem esse reipsa fundamentum & radicem aedificii & fructus spiritualis, non esse intelligendum de quocunque actu fidei, sed de eo qui ita congruit cum affectu, ut ipsum excitet & moveat. Fides autem quae affectum non movet, neque ex se actuosa est, ut alliciat voluntatem ad bonum, non habet rationem radicis & fundamenti, saltem actu, tametsi vera fides dicenda sit. Tom. 2. in primam secundae, Difput. 210. cap. 7. num. 54. Quibus consona sunt quae supra citavimus ex Stapletono, dum ait, Per fidem quae nondum formata est impetrari charitatem qua postea formetur, si tamen id fiat quod fides suggerit, id est, si oratio fidei adhibeatur. De Justif. lib. 8. cap. 17.
pass_a_gloss: When Roman theologians say even not-yet-formed faith is justifying in its way because it disposes to justification and is the root and foundation of a person justice before God, by not-yet-formed faith they do not mean inert idle faith that is merely speculative, but a certain active faith that begins to be effective through good works, somehow births charity, and strives toward it, though it cannot yet be said to have attained it. Vasquez teaches this openly: when we say faith is really the foundation and root of the spiritual building and fruit, we do not mean every act of faith, but that act which so agrees with affection that it stirs and moves it; faith that does not move affection and is not of itself active so as to draw the will to the good does not have the character of root and foundation, at least in act, even if it may be called true faith (Tom. 2 in 1a 2ae, Disp. 210, c. 7, n. 54). Stapleton agrees: through not-yet-formed faith charity is obtained by which it is later formed, if what faith suggests is done, if the prayer of faith is used (De Justif. 8.17).
pass_b_english: When Romans call not-yet-formed faith justifying as root and foundation, they do not mean idle speculative faith, but an active faith that begins to work through good works, somehow generates charity, and presses toward it without yet fully possessing it.

Vasquez: only the faith-act that stirs affection counts as root and foundation in act (Disp. 210.7.54); Stapleton likewise ties not-yet-formed faith to obtaining charity through the prayer faith prompts (De Justif. 8.17).

choices.why: Roman unformed-but-disposing faith is not mere speculation.
rejected: any speculative assent as justifying disposition
